title: Noise investigation scratchpad (Q1 2026 perf baseline)
body:
Context
- This is a running scratchpad for variance/noise investigations for the “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” (Q1 2026).
- Goal: reduce false regressions + improve reproducibility. Not trying to “optimize” performance here; trying to make it stable + explainable.
- Primary metrics we’re watching during noise work:
  - TTFT p50/p95/p99 (streaming and non-streaming definitions per ADR-0172)
  - TPOT p50/p95/p99
  - Throughput tokens/s (and req/s for embeddings)
  - Secondary explanatory metrics (from runtime instrumentation): scheduler queue wait, batch assembly time, batch size distribution, cache hit signals.

Baseline reminder
- Hardware targets: H100, A100, L40S (as available) in us-east + eu-west.
- Workloads: chat streaming, long-context prefill stress, tool/function calling burstiness, embeddings high-QPS.
- Decision we keep revisiting: report both cold + warm cache scenarios (see slack:eng-runtime/1764196509). This interacts heavily with variance.

Noise sources: hypotheses checklist
(Keeping this list to quickly annotate suspicious runs in the tracker)
1) GPU clocks / power management state drift
2) GPU thermals + multi-tenant contention (even if “dedicated” node, shared rack variance)
3) Container placement / host-level CPU contention
4) NUMA + CPU pinning (prefill CPU overhead + networking + driver threads)
5) Warmup / autotuning / kernel compilation (first-run effects)
6) Kernel auto-selection nondeterminism or “threshold” cliffs (seq length bin boundary)
7) Cache effects (prefix/KV cache, allocator fragmentation)
8) Network jitter + client read behavior (especially streaming pacing)
9) Batch formation sensitivity (arrival patterns, scheduler backpressure)
10) Background daemons / telemetry overhead / noisy neighbor in cluster control plane

Quick summary of what seems to matter most (as of 2026-02-14)
- Biggest drivers of p99 TTFT variance:
  - GPU clock state not pinned + node warm state (can swing p99 TTFT meaningfully on long-prefill)
  - Placement differences (host CPU contention + NUMA locality) affecting prefill pipeline and scheduler threads
  - Kernel selection cliffs around sequence length regimes (especially prefill-heavy runs)
- Biggest drivers of TPOT variance:
  - Batch size distribution shift due to arrival jitter / concurrency ramp config
  - GPU clocks (smaller effect than TTFT but non-trivial)
- Embeddings variance:
  - Mostly CPU/network + request generator scheduling (req/s can wobble if the loadgen is not isolated)

Experiment log (lightweight, mostly “try something and write down what changed”)

Exp 1: GPU clocks locked vs default
- Trigger: saw repeated p99 TTFT outliers on H100 long-prefill even with same runtime SHA + same workload seed.
- Setup:
  - Same model + workload seed, same concurrency target, same region, same container image.
  - Change: enable persistence + lock application clocks (where allowed by fleet policy).
- Observation:
  - Variance reduced noticeably (especially p99 TTFT). Mean moved slightly faster too, but we’re not optimizing here.
  - Without locking: runs sometimes start “slow” and stabilize after a few minutes; with locking: less ramp artifact.
- Notes:
  - Need to ensure we’re not violating any shared cluster policies.
  - Action: add manifest fields capturing (a) persistence mode, (b) clocks locked yes/no, (c) observed clocks during run (sampled).
- TODO:
  - Standardize “clock state capture” into harness preflight and persist into run manifest.

Exp 2: Warmup standardization (prefill + decode) before measuring
- Trigger: first 1–2 minutes of a run shows higher TTFT and different kernel mix; suspected lazy init, autotune, memory allocator.
- Setup:
  - Apply fixed warmup phase: N requests per workload scenario before measurement window.
  - Warmup requests use same shape distribution but are excluded from reported metrics.
- Observation:
  - Reduced run-to-run drift; eliminated some “first batch huge” artifacts.
  - On some models, warmup cost is higher (initial graph / kernel caching). But measurement is more stable.
- Where captured:
  - Implemented in github:benchmark-lab/pr-21471-add-long-context-prefill-workload-and-warmup.
- Open question:
  - Should warmup be part of every workload (chat/embeddings) or only long-context? Current leaning: yes for all, but smaller warmup for embeddings.

Exp 3: Container placement + CPU isolation
- Trigger: embeddings req/s and chat TTFT swings without corresponding GPU utilization change; suggests CPU-side bottleneck variability.
- Setup:
  - Compare runs on same GPU SKU with:
    A) default k8s node scheduling
    B) pinned to “benchmark” node pool with cpu-manager static + guaranteed QoS
    C) explicit CPU pinning for runtime + load generator on separate hosts
- Observation:
  - B is better than A (less tail weirdness).
  - C is best but operationally heavier.
  - When loadgen shares host with runtime, p99 TTFT and TPOT can reflect loadgen pauses (GC / scheduling), especially for streaming.
- Action:
  - For baseline sweeps: require load generator on separate node, and runtime container guaranteed QoS.
  - Add manifest fields: node pool, cpu-manager policy, container QoS class, and whether loadgen is colocated.

Exp 4: NUMA locality + NIC affinity
- Trigger: long-prefill p99 TTFT shifts + strange CPU time spikes, especially on dual-socket hosts.
- Setup:
  - Run with and without explicit NUMA binding (runtime process + network interrupts affinity) on the benchmark node pool.
- Observation:
  - On dual-socket nodes, binding can reduce variance. Unbound runs sometimes hop memory causing occasional spikes.
- Caveat:
  - Our fleet is not fully homogeneous; pinning assumptions can break if topology differs.
- Action:
  - Minimum: record NUMA topology and affinity settings in manifest (even if we don’t enforce pinning everywhere).

Exp 5: Kernel selection “cliff” at sequence length boundaries
- Trigger: identical workloads but slightly different prompt length bins produce disproportionate TTFT changes; suspicion: kernel auto-selection threshold.
- Setup:
  - Sweep prompt lengths around bin boundaries used by kernel selection.
  - Compare kernel debug dump outputs.
- Observation:
  - Some regimes flip kernels and show measurable TTFT changes; can appear as noise if workload distribution slightly shifts.
- Follow-up:
  - Enable kernel selection debug dumps for perf runs (github:redwood/pr-21519-add-kernel-selection-debug-dump-for-perf-runs).
  - For baseline freezing, consider pinning known-good kernel for affected model/SKU until auto-selection is stabilized (see slack:eng-runtime/1764699022).

Exp 6: Cache effects (cold vs warm) and allocator state
- Trigger: debate on whether caching belongs in baselines + difficulty comparing runs when caches are in different states.
- Setup:
  - Explicit “cold” mode: ensure no prefix/KV cache reuse across requests; restart runtime between trials.
  - Explicit “warm” mode: pre-seed with a fixed prompt prefix set; run steady-state and report metrics separately.
- Observation:
  - Cold mode is more comparable across code changes but more sensitive to startup and warmup handling.
  - Warm mode resembles production for many cohorts but is more sensitive to cache policies/eviction changes; can be legitimately impacted by runtime changes.
- Decision (tentative, aligns w/ slack:eng-runtime/1764196509):
  - Report both cold and warm for baseline suite; gating thresholds may differ by mode.
- TODO:
  - Define cache seeding procedure per workload with explicit seed + prompt-set hash in manifest.

Exp 7: Client read behavior contaminating streaming TTFT/TPOT
- Trigger: streaming metrics differ depending on client implementation; risk we’re measuring client backpressure.
- Setup:
  - Compare:
    - “fast read” client (drains stream as quickly as possible)
    - “paced read” client (simulates UI)
    - server-side timestamping for token emission (if available)
- Observation:
  - Paced read inflates apparent TPOT. Some TTFT definitions can be affected if client doesn’t read promptly.
- Action:
  - For baseline + gating: use fast-read client. For product realism: optionally keep paced-read scenario as a non-gating informational panel.
  - Ensure metric definition is explicit: TTFT = first token on wire from server timestamp vs first token observed by client. Current baseline uses client-observed; we should add server-side emission timestamp when possible.
- Reference: slack:eng-runtime/1763935150.

Exp 8: Concurrency ramp + arrival process sensitivity
- Trigger: small changes in ramp parameters shift batch size distributions; can look like throughput regression.
- Setup:
  - Run fixed concurrency vs ramp-to-target; compare batch histograms and p99.
- Observation:
  - Ramp is closer to real traffic but introduces extra variance; fixed concurrency is more stable for kernel/scheduler regression detection.
- Proposed compromise:
  - Baseline “stable” mode for gating uses fixed concurrency after warmup.
  - Representative suite includes a ramp scenario but with looser thresholds.

Instrumentation notes (what we need to attribute variance)
- Must-have tags on every metric export (so dashboards can slice):
  - model_id, model_family, model_revision
  - gpu_sku, host_type, region
  - workload_id, scenario (cold/warm), streaming_mode
  - runtime_git_sha, build_id, compiler/triton/cuda versions
  - scheduler_policy_id + key knobs
  - kernel_selection_profile_id (and debug dump pointer)
- Runtime metrics requested/implemented:
  - scheduler queue wait time distribution
  - batch assembly time + batch size histogram
  - load-shed/drop counters
  - KV cache hit-ish signals (or at least eviction counters / occupancy)
  - kernel selection chosen + fallback reason (sampled)
- References:
  - github:redwood/pr-21503-scheduler-queue-time-and-batch-assembly-metrics
  - linear:ENG-4826

Noise model thoughts (for Sana)
- For each (model, workload, region, SKU, scenario), we should treat noise as a distribution, not a single number.
- For gating:
  - Need minimum sample sizes (number of runs and/or total requests) to estimate p99 with enough confidence.
  - Prefer comparing distributions via robust stats (median of p95 across runs, or bootstrap CI) rather than one-off run deltas.
- “Regression vs noise” rough heuristics (NOT FINAL):
  - p99 TTFT: very sensitive; require more runs and/or larger thresholds than p50.
  - Throughput tokens/s: can be stable if arrival process fixed; otherwise track batch histogram drift.
- Action item:
  - Draft per-workload “expected coefficient of variation” from baseline sweep data; store in perf-regression-policy doc.

Operational guardrails for baseline sweeps (proposed)
- Always record:
  - node hostname + instance id
  - GPU clocks (observed) + persistence mode
  - CPU topology summary (sockets, NUMA nodes)
  - container QoS + cpu-manager policy
  - loadgen location (same host? same rack? separate cluster?)
  - network path hints (region/az)
- Always do:
  - warmup phase
  - fixed measurement window length
  - fixed workload seed
  - fast-read streaming client
- Avoid (unless explicitly testing it):
  - mixing kernel selection changes with scheduler changes in the same “noise” experiment
  - running baseline jobs concurrently on same node pool without isolation

Open questions / TODOs
- Should we enforce clock locking for ALL baseline runs or only H100? (Needs SRE signoff + policy.)
- How to represent “host cleanliness” in manifest (e.g., no other pods, reserved node) without exposing internal infra details?
- Do we need separate “GC mode” for Python loadgen (or move more loadgen to Go/Rust) to reduce jitter?
- For eu-west vs us-east: are we seeing real region effects or just different node pools? Need controlled A/B with identical host types.

Pointers (where to check data)
- Baseline run tracker: drive:shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/q1-2026-baseline-run-tracker.json
- Most relevant Slack discussions:
  - Fleet variance / warmup / isolation: slack:eng-sre/1763512044
  - p99 regression triage for long-prefill: slack:eng-runtime/1763608899
  - Caching in baselines: slack:eng-runtime/1764196509

Notes to self
- When a run looks “slow”: first check kernel selection dump + GPU clocks + batch histogram BEFORE assuming runtime regression.
- If p99 regresses but p50 is flat: suspect queueing/backpressure or placement, not kernel math.
- Keep a list of “known flaky nodes” (privately) but do not bake that into published methodology; instead enforce isolation + manifests so we can explain it.
